records.originEnglish: Abraham our father, of blessed memory, had the quality of love of the blessed God, as it is written, “The offspring of Abraham, My beloved.” This quality consists in walking from level to level, becoming more fully refined in that quality each time. Thus it is written, “I will give you those who walk among these who stand”: the angels stand, whereas a person must always be walking from one level to another. Similarly, we find that Moses our teacher said, “I can no longer go out and come in.” He was saying that he no longer had any occupation in this world: since he could not go out, he could not enter a higher level.

records.targetEnglish: Therefore he said, “I will give you those who walk among these who stand” (Zechariah 3:7). The angels are called those who stand, for they cannot walk: since they cannot go out, they cannot come in either. The souls of the righteous are called those who walk. This is what Rabbi Meir meant by Israel’s first advantage: they are guarded, while the angels are the guardians and do not need to be guarded. Needing to be guarded can itself be an advantage; the angels, by contrast, guard and are not guarded. The proof is not that, because they guard Israel, they are subordinate to them. After all, we also find, “The Lord is your guardian” (Psalms 121:5), and, in Vayetzei, “I will guard you wherever you go” (Genesis 28:15). Rather, he meant that the angels possess the power of guarding without having any fear that would require them to be guarded as well. Every created being that possesses an advantage also has a corresponding deficiency, which it fears and against which it needs protection. For the angels to have the power of guarding without any possibility of going out into harm is itself a deficiency. This reasoning does not apply to the blessed God.
records.explanation: This passage explains the unusually sharp connection between “going out” and “coming in” in Lech Lecha. A created being that cannot leave its present station also cannot reach a higher one. The need for protection therefore need not negate human spiritual dignity; it accompanies the capacity to grow. Rav Tzadok explicitly limits this argument to created beings and rejects the inference that every guardian must be lower than the one it guards.

records.targetEnglish: The meaning is as my revered grandfather, of blessed memory, explained. The service of the angels on high cannot truly be credited to them as their own achievement, because they have no choice to act against His will and no obstacles they must overcome. They do not even desire what is outside His will, as it is said of them, “Wherever the spirit would go, they would go; they did not turn as they went” (Ezekiel 1:12). They have no inclination toward what is outside His will, so their service cannot be called the labor of their own hands. This is what the angels’ banners signify: their service follows a fixed order, in which they can neither lose nor gain. Israel is different: “I will give you those who walk among these who stand” (Zechariah 3:7). Israel is called one who walks, able to go from level to level without being confined to one fixed order, and able to gain through its service. It is true that it can also lose, God forbid, but it can also gain. This explains Israel’s desire for banners: everything they had acquired through their service should be established in an order that would prevent its loss. Yet they also wished to remain walkers, able to acquire more. Their principal wish to resemble the angels was that they should not lose what they had already acquired.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef develops the same contrast between walkers and those who stand into a precise account of spiritual achievement. Advancement becomes one’s own work because it involves resistance and choice. Israel’s desire for banners then adds a useful distinction to Rav Tzadok’s demand for continuing growth: one may seek stability in what has already been acquired while still seeking a higher level. The passage does not ask a person to become immobile like an angel.

records.reverseThemeTitle: Retaining what one has earned while remaining able to grow
records.reverseThemeSummary: Israel’s desire for the angels’ banners seeks security in what service has already attained, while preserving the human ability to move to a higher level. A fixed order alone would remove both loss and gain.
records.reverseExplanation: Peri Tzadik gives the movement between levels its direction: Abraham repeatedly refines his love of God. His reading of Moses’ inability to “go out and come in” explains why losing the possibility of movement would also remove the possibility of higher attainment. This makes clear why the banners desired in Tiferet Yosef secure what has been earned without making Israel stationary.

records.originEnglish: This corresponds to what is said, “Your eyes shall see your teachers”: from everything one sees, one should learn something for the service of the blessed God. Certainly this sight was not shown to him for nothing, but so that he should learn the way of God from it. Similarly, from what he hears he should learn the ways of service, as it is said, “Your ears shall hear a word behind you, [saying,] ‘This is the way; walk in it.’” He should know that the blessed God did not arrange for him to hear this thing for nothing; it was certainly so that he should learn God’s way from it. This is what they said: “Who is wise? One who learns from every person.” He learns from everything he hears and sees, even when the other person does not intend to teach him. Abraham attained this after circumcision, becoming a new creation whose eyes and ears would see and hear only a matter of mitzvah, learning the way of God.
records.themeTitle: Learning Divine service from what one sees and hears
records.themeSummary: The refinement of Abraham’s senses means that an encounter becomes instruction in Divine service, even when no one intended to teach. The relevant question is what this particular encounter can teach.
records.targetHebrew: וְיֵשׁ גַּם כֵּן לִכְלַל יִשְׂרָאֵל אֲחִיזָה בַּתּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה, דַּאֲפִילּוּ כָּל עַם הָאָרֶץ שֶׁבְּיִשְׂרָאֵל יֵשׁ בָּהֶם מְצִיאוּת אֵיזֶה דָבָר שֶׁל חָכְמָה שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ שַׁיָּכוּת לְתוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה, רַק שֶׁהוּא אֶצְלוֹ בְּתַכְלִית הַהֶעְלֵם; וְלֶעָתִיד נֶאֱמַר: "כִּי כֻלָּם יֵדְעוּ [אוֹתִי לְמִקְּטַנָּם וְעַד גְּדוֹלָם]" [יִרְמְיָהוּ ל״א:ל״ג], שֶׁיֵּצֵא הַיְּדִיעָה שֶׁבָּהֶם מֵהַהֶעְלֵם לְגִלּוּי. וְעַל כֵּן אָמְרוּ בַּזֹּהַר [חֵלֶק ג׳ קס״ז עַמּוּד ב׳] דְּגַם מִילֵּי דְּהֶדְיוֹטָא מִלָּה הִיא, וְזִמְנִין דִּבְאַפְרַכְסְתָא דַּעַנְיָא מִשְׁתַּכַּח מַרְגָּנִיתָא; וּבַגְּמָרָא בְּכָל דּוּכְתָּא: הַיְינוּ דְּאָמְרֵי אֱינָשֵׁי, שֶׁהֵם דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה; וּבְפֶרֶק קַמָּא דְּסַנְהֶדְרִין (ו׳ עַמּוּד א׳): הַהוּא דַּהֲוָה אָמַר וְאָזֵיל, וְהֵם דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, וְכֵן בְּכָל דּוּכְתָּא. וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ (אָבוֹת פֶּרֶק ד׳ מִשְׁנָה א׳): "אֵיזֶהוּ חָכָם? הַלּוֹמֵד מִכָּל אָדָם", דִּבְכָל אָדָם יֵשׁ אֵיזֶה דָּבָר הִתְחַדְּשׁוּת שֶׁל חָכְמָה הַשַּׁיָּךְ לְשֹׁרֶשׁ נַפְשׁוֹ בְּיִחוּד שֶׁיֵּשׁ לִלְמֹד מִמֶּנּוּ; וְ"אַתֶּם קְרוּיִין אָדָם, וְאֵין אֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם קְרוּיִין אָדָם" [יְבָמוֹת ס״א עַמּוּד א׳], דְּרַק בְּכָל אֶחָד מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל יֵשׁ אֵיזֶה דָבָר פְּרָטִי מִתּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה הַשַּׁיָּךְ לְשֹׁרֶשׁ נַפְשׁוֹ, וְהַמֵּבִין יָכוֹל לִלְמֹד זֶה מִמֶּנּוּ אַף שֶׁהוּא עַצְמוֹ אֵינוֹ יוֹדֵעַ כְּלוּם, אֲבָל מְבַקְשֵׁי ה' יָבִינוּ כֹל [מִשְׁלֵי כ״ח:ה׳], וְיַשִּׂיגוּ מִתּוֹךְ שִׂיחוֹתָיו וְדִבּוּרָיו בְּעִנְיְנֵי הָעוֹלָם אֵיזֶה דָבָר שֶׁל חָכְמָה שֶׁבְּשֹׁרֶשׁ נַפְשׁוֹ הַמִּתְעַלֵּם בָּזֶה.
records.targetEnglish: The community of Israel also has a hold in the Oral Torah. Even every unlearned person in Israel possesses some element of wisdom that belongs to the Oral Torah, although in him it is entirely concealed. Concerning the future it is said, “They shall all know [Me, from the least of them to the greatest]” (Jeremiah 31:33): the knowledge within them will emerge from concealment into revelation. Therefore the Zohar says that even an ordinary person’s words may be significant, and sometimes a pearl is found in a poor person’s basket. Throughout the Talmud we find, “This is what people say,” and their sayings are words of Torah; likewise the first chapter of Sanhedrin (6a) cites “a certain person who used to say,” and these are words of Torah. This is what they said, “Who is wise? One who learns from every person” (Avot 4:1): each person has some new element of wisdom that belongs particularly to the root of his soul and can be learned from him. “You are called adam, whereas the nations of the world are not called adam” (Yevamot 61a): here the point is that each member of Israel has a particular element of Oral Torah belonging to his soul’s root. A discerning person can learn it from him even if he himself knows nothing of it. But “those who seek the Lord understand everything” (Proverbs 28:5), and they can discern, through his conversations and words about worldly matters, some wisdom of his soul’s root that is concealed within them.
records.explanation: Poked Akarim explains how someone can teach without intending to do so. Ordinary speech can carry an insight that its speaker has not recognized, while a discerning listener brings it to light. Rav Tzadok frames this explanation specifically through Israel’s relation to Oral Torah; it is not a claim here that every casual remark is authoritative Torah. It clarifies why the listener’s refined attention, rather than the speaker’s intention to teach, is central to the Lech Lecha passage.

records.originEnglish: This corresponds to what is said, “Your eyes shall see your teachers”: from everything one sees, one should learn something for the service of the blessed God. Certainly this sight was not shown to him for nothing, but so that he should learn the way of God from it. Similarly, from what he hears he should learn the ways of service, as it is said, “Your ears shall hear a word behind you, [saying,] ‘This is the way; walk in it.’” He should know that the blessed God did not arrange for him to hear this thing for nothing; it was certainly so that he should learn God’s way from it. This is what they said: “Who is wise? One who learns from every person.” He learns from everything he hears and sees, even when the other person does not intend to teach him. Abraham attained this after circumcision, becoming a new creation whose eyes and ears would see and hear only a matter of mitzvah, learning the way of God.

records.targetEnglish: The meaning is this: when Abraham saw that they give way before one another, he understood that the blessed God had not concealed Himself completely. He had therefore established two opposites, so that through both of them people would recognize that there is One above them who rules them, and would direct their attention only to Him. For this reason the blessed God also established male and female throughout the world. Likewise it is written, “Lift your eyes on high and see: Who created these?” (Isaiah 40:26). “These” means all the particulars that the blessed God established in the world. “Who” is the place that stands open to questioning: a person should seek to know who created these. For this purpose the blessed God created all the particulars called “these.” As is taught in the introduction to the holy Zohar (1b), and as was explained in Bereishit, the blessed God desires that created beings ask who the Creator is. He therefore created opposing things in the world.
records.explanation: Beit Yaakov supplies a concrete model for learning from a sight. Abraham observes the sun and moon giving way to one another; the limits of each prompt him to seek the One who governs both. Created particulars are therefore occasions for an attentive question about their source. This makes Rav Tzadok’s “not shown to him for nothing” more precise: the encounter should lead to recognition and service, rather than merely to a free association imposed on what one sees.

records.reverseThemeTitle: Created particulars invite recognition of their Creator
records.reverseThemeSummary: Abraham learns from the limits and oppositions among created things. Their particulars prompt the question “Who created these?” and call for conscious recognition rather than a substitute that bypasses the person’s own service.
records.reverseExplanation: Peri Tzadik turns the attentive observation described in Beit Yaakov into a developed account of the senses: everything seen or heard can become instruction in Divine service, even without an intentional human teacher. Abraham’s recognition through the sun and moon is therefore a concrete instance of the way of learning that Rav Tzadok attributes to refined sight and hearing.

records.originEnglish: This is the meaning of “Yours is the dew of your youth”: it is the dew of Atika, the Ancient One. It corresponds to what they said (Shabbat 89b): “If your sins are like years”—like these years that have been ordered and have come from the six days of Creation until now—“they shall become white as snow.” Through repentance from love it becomes clear that in the utterance “Bereishit,” in which “And He said” does not appear and which signifies an understanding concealed from every conception, “formlessness and emptiness” had already been mentioned. These allude to the deeds of the wicked, as is taught in Bereishit Rabbah. This was the intention: first darkness, then light, so that light should gain its advantage from within darkness. It corresponds to the Zohar’s statement (II, 184a), “There is no light except that which emerges from darkness.” Then “they shall become white as snow”: they become merits. This is the meaning of “Yours is the dew of your youth”: it was the blessed God’s intention that the forty-eight years should come first and that afterward Abraham our father should recognize his Creator. records.targetEnglish: The essence of repentance is to reach the point at which God illuminates one’s eyes so that deliberate sins become merits. That is, one recognizes and understands that everything in which one sinned was also within the will of the blessed God, as our Sages said (Berakhot 31b), “Three verses …,” including “You turned their hearts backward” and “Whom I afflicted.” This follows the meaning of Divine knowledge and human choice explained by the Ari at the end of the book Arba Me’ot Shekel Kesef: both are true, each in its own domain. In the domain of choice there is no place for knowledge, and in the domain of knowledge there is truly no place for choice. When one attains this immense light, all one’s deliberate sins turn out not to have fallen outside the depth of the blessed God’s knowledge; He, His knowledge, and His will are all one. Since the blessed God willed it so, everything is a merit, and one attains the complete atonement of Yom Kippur. This is the secret of the goat sent to Azazel. If a person had performed this on his own initiative, he would have been an outright idolater: it would fall under “You shall have no other gods,” the foundation of all prohibitions and of all transgressions and departures from the blessed God’s will. But because the goat is sent by the blessed God’s will—He commands that it be sent there—it becomes a mitzvah rather than a transgression. Thus our Sages explained it (Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer 46); see also Ramban on Acharei. We give a portion to Azazel, which is evil, because the blessed God commanded us to give it to him. Thus what would be a transgression becomes a mitzvah.
records.explanation: Tzidkat HaTzadik explains the difficult claim that the past can become merit. The recognition belongs to the light attained through repentance, while the domain of human choice retains its own truth. The example of Azazel sharply preserves the distinction between a Divine command and a person’s private initiative. Read beside Lech Lecha, it prevents “this was the intention” from becoming a prospective justification for wrongdoing.

records.reverseExplanation: Peri Tzadik supplies Abraham’s youth as a concrete setting for the difficult retrospective claim in Tzidkat HaTzadik. It illustrates the transformation after return while leaving intact the distinction between human choice and the illumination of Divine knowledge.

It corresponds to what they said (Shabbat 89b): “If your sins are like years”—like these years that have been ordered and have come from the six days of Creation until now—“they shall become white as snow.” Through repentance from love it becomes clear that in the utterance “Bereishit,” in which “And He said” does not appear and which signifies an understanding concealed from every conception, “formlessness and emptiness” had already been mentioned. These allude to the deeds of the wicked, as is taught in Bereishit Rabbah. This was the intention: first darkness, then light, so that light should gain its advantage from within darkness. It corresponds to the Zohar’s statement (II, 184a), “There is no light except that which emerges from darkness.” Then “they shall become white as snow”: they become merits. records.targetEnglish: When a person deepens his service, he then truly sees that all the places in which he stood very far from the blessed God are filled with light. This is what the Talmud teaches (Yoma 86b): when one returns from love, deliberate sins become merits. After the repentance by which he returns to God through great labor in His service, he truly sees that what had previously appeared to him as a position of great distance was filled with His will. This explains the midrash quoted above: Cain answered Adam, “I repented and reached a settlement,” whereupon Adam began, “A psalm, a song for the Sabbath day.” For one attains this recognition fully on Shabbat. Then, when Shabbat comes, rest comes: one sees and explicitly recognizes that every place is full of light. As the Talmud says (Megillah 12b), “The seventh day was Shabbat”: the nations of the world eat and drink and begin indecent talk, while Israel begins songs and praises. My revered grandfather, of blessed memory, explained that the day itself causes this. On this day, as we say, “On the seventh day He rose and sat upon His throne of glory,” the nations say that this confirms their view that, God forbid, God has abandoned the earth, and they give themselves still greater license. Israel is different: on Shabbat it explicitly recognizes that all its power comes from the blessed God—even the power of repentance comes from the blessed God—and that the blessed God governs His world. It then explicitly recognizes that every place is filled with the light of the blessed God.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef connects the same two elements that structure this ois: repentance from love and the recognition available on Shabbat. The former distance is seen differently only after a return accomplished through serious service. His closing contrast expressly rejects the inference that Divine transcendence means the world has been abandoned to human indulgence. This illuminates why Rav Tzadok places Abraham’s transformed past within the Shabbat meal’s light.

records.originEnglish: The Tanchuma there says: “You find that everyone who is exacting about the mitzvot receives a great reward. Thus we find that Abraham was exacting about the mitzvot, and therefore he was called the beloved of the Holy One, blessed be He. … He observed even eruv tavshilin. … ‘And My teachings’—are there then many Torahs? … These are the fine details of the mitzvot.” That is, the Oral Torah is called the fine details of the mitzvot. In the Written Torah only the general commandment is mentioned, while in the Oral Torah an entire tractate and many laws are arranged around it. This is why the plural “My teachings” is interpreted as referring to Oral Torah. Likewise, earlier in the Tanchuma, in Noach, it says: “He gave us the Written Torah in allusion, and they explained it through the Oral Torah. … The Written Torah gives the general principles, and the Oral Torah the particulars.” It then says of the Oral Torah, with its fine details of lighter and weightier mitzvot, that only someone who loves the Holy One, blessed be He, with all his heart, all his soul, and all his might studies it; see there.
records.themeTitle: Love gives the strength to study the details
records.themeSummary: Abraham’s love appears in exacting attention to the mitzvot. Rav Tzadok identifies this with Oral Torah, whose sustained study unfolds the particulars contained in the Written Torah’s general commands.
records.targetHebrew: וּפוּרִים הוּא הַתְחָלַת תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה עַל יְדֵי דְּ"הָדַר קִבְּלוּהָ מֵאַהֲבָה" (שַׁבָּת פ״ח עַמּוּד א׳), וְתֹקֶף הַחֵשֶׁק, שֶׁזֶּהוּ יְסוֹד תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה, כְּפִי גֹּדֶל הַחֵשֶׁק וְהָאַהֲבָה שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ לְדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה לִמְסֹר נַפְשׁוֹ עָלֶיהָ, כֵּן הוּא הַשָּׂגַת חָכְמָתוֹ וְהַמִּסְטוֹרִין הַמִּתְגַּלִּין לוֹ מֵהַמְשָׁכַת חָכְמָה עֶלְיוֹנָה (עַיֵּן זֹהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ חֵלֶק ב׳ פ״ה עַמּוּד א׳) שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה מֵהַבִּינָה וְהַדַּעַת דִּידִיעַת וְהַשָּׂגַת אָדָם;
records.targetEnglish: Purim is the beginning of Oral Torah, through their “accepting it again from love” (Shabbat 88a) and through the intensity of their desire. This is the foundation of Oral Torah: in proportion to the greatness of a person’s desire and love for words of Torah, to the point of giving himself over to it, so is his attainment of its wisdom and of the mysteries revealed to him through an influx of supernal wisdom (see Zohar II, 85a), which is above the understanding and knowledge of human cognition and attainment.
records.explanation: Divrei Soferim makes explicit why love matters for the detailed study described here: sustained desire and the willingness to devote oneself to Torah shape what one can receive from it. Oral Torah’s particulars are therefore more than technical additions to a general command. Their disclosure involves both demanding human devotion and wisdom received from above.

records.originEnglish: At first, the five occurrences of “light” in the utterance “Let there be light” corresponded to the five books of the Torah, as is taught in Bereishit Rabbah. Afterward the first light was hidden away for those who labor in Oral Torah, as is taught in the Tanchuma in Noach. Concerning Oral Torah it is said, “May my utterance flow like dew.” As we have explained, Oral Torah is compared to dew: when dew descends, its descent from heaven is not visible; one understands that it fell only upon seeing the earth wet. Similarly, it appears to the sages that they are originating insights in their hearts, but in truth these are the word of God—“My words that I have placed in your mouth”—and they come from the dew of Atika. Abraham our father attained this: his two kidneys poured forth wisdom that God had prepared for him, as is taught in Bereishit Rabbah. This is what was said to him, “Yours is the dew of your youth.” Shabbat too is the seventh quality, Malkhut: “the mouth, which we call Oral Torah.” It is the time to merit Torah, particularly at the meal of Atika.
records.themeTitle: Torah insight as a revelation received through the mind
records.themeSummary: The dew image holds human thought and Divine revelation together: the sages genuinely discover Torah, while its deeper source is not produced by their private will.

records.targetEnglish: The meaning is as taught in Mei HaShiloach: “If you have become wise, you have become wise for yourself.” If you have arrived at new words of Torah, “you have become wise for yourself”: all the newness is on your side. You have added nothing new to the Torah itself, for this too was truly included in it; until now it was simply hidden and concealed from you. Our Sages carefully interpreted every extra letter and point in the Torah. Could it enter your heart that they invented this and that it was not previously included in Torah? In truth it was included in Torah from beginning to end. Only from the person’s side was this new insight closed and sealed until now; now he too has arrived at it. One must not imagine that they added anything to Torah. As is taught in Ta’anit 9a and in Shemot Rabbah, Yitro 28:6, all prophecy is alluded to in the Torah of Moses, indicating that nothing has been newly added to Torah. “But if you scoff, you alone will bear it”: if you wish to bring yourself a proof from Torah for something that does not accord with the blessed God’s will, you alone will bear that twisted and crooked interpretation. Do not imagine that you can insert such an interpretation into Torah. As the Tanchuma teaches (Tazria 9), “‘Evil will not dwell with You’—evil does not drag You along.” Words of Torah rise above and stand apart in their clarity; no twisted interpretation enters them.
records.explanation: Beit Yaakov explains the distinction contained in the dew metaphor: an insight is new to its discoverer while already belonging to Torah. His second reading supplies an essential boundary. A person cannot make a desired conclusion into Torah merely by finding words that appear to support it. Together the passages distinguish authentic discovery from a private invention that contradicts the Divine will.

records.reverseThemeTitle: Discovering Torah without bending it to a private desire
records.reverseThemeSummary: The newness of an insight belongs to the learner’s discovery. Torah already contains its true insights and cannot be made to endorse a crooked interpretation that conflicts with the Divine will.
records.reverseExplanation: Peri Tzadik’s dew image explains how a discovery may arise within the scholar’s mind while having a source beyond that mind. This gives an account of the authentic innovation affirmed by Beit Yaakov. Read with Beit Yaakov’s express warning about crooked interpretations, the image concerns the revelation of Torah and does not authorize every private thought as God’s word.

records.originEnglish: At first, the five occurrences of “light” in the utterance “Let there be light” corresponded to the five books of the Torah, as is taught in Bereishit Rabbah. Afterward the first light was hidden away for those who labor in Oral Torah, as is taught in the Tanchuma in Noach. Concerning Oral Torah it is said, “May my utterance flow like dew.” As we have explained, Oral Torah is compared to dew: when dew descends, its descent from heaven is not visible; one understands that it fell only upon seeing the earth wet. Similarly, it appears to the sages that they are originating insights in their hearts, but in truth these are the word of God—“My words that I have placed in your mouth”—and they come from the dew of Atika. Abraham our father attained this: his two kidneys poured forth wisdom that God had prepared for him, as is taught in Bereishit Rabbah. This is what was said to him, “Yours is the dew of your youth.” Shabbat too is the seventh quality, Malkhut: “the mouth, which we call Oral Torah.” It is the time to merit Torah, particularly at the meal of Atika.
records.themeTitle: Torah insight as a revelation received through the mind
records.themeSummary: The dew image holds human thought and Divine revelation together: the sages genuinely discover Torah, while its deeper source is not produced by their private will.

records.targetEnglish: This proceeds through the prior awakening from below, with intense desire. At this initial stage, as explained above in section 184, one is called “My daughter.” Afterward, when an awakening from above comes to assist, new insights arise for him and awe is born, as explained above; then one is called “My sister,” and they unite, as the Zohar explains the verse, “She is indeed my sister … and she became my wife” (Genesis 20:12). It is through recognizing that the new insights come from the blessed God—this is humility and acting for its own sake, recognizing that he has nothing of his own—that there is success and he rises to the greatness of being called “My mother.” This follows the rule that, after the blessing and the recognition that everything comes from the blessed God, the blessed God then says that everything belongs to the person: even the awakening from above is his. This is the meaning of “Give strength”—that is, words of Torah, as explained above—“to God” (Psalms 68:35), for it was through his awakening from below that this came into being.
records.explanation: Tzidkat HaTzadik describes the process behind the dew: intense human desire precedes assistance from above, and the scholar’s recognition of that source is itself part of the attainment. The familial images culminate in “My mother,” the person credited with bringing Torah into the world. This gives precise content to Rav Tzadok’s claim that the sages both innovate in their hearts and receive God’s words.
records.translationProvenance: New English translations of the quoted Hebrew prepared for this reviewed thematic connection. Hebrew quotations are retained from the canonical Akiva Publishing text; the complete origin section and complete target paragraph were read in context. These are editorial connections, not claims that one author explicitly cites the other.
records.reverseThemeTitle: Receiving new Torah through longing and humility
records.reverseThemeSummary: Torah gives strength against the inclination, and its innovations arise through human longing and assistance from above. Recognizing that source makes it possible for what is received to become the person’s own Torah.
records.reverseExplanation: Peri Tzadik provides a concrete image for the movement described through “daughter,” “sister,” and “mother”: dew is known from its effect although its descent was not observed. In the same way, an insight can appear as the scholar’s innovation while being a Divine gift. The image clarifies the recognition on which Tzidkat HaTzadik makes the scholar’s subsequent attainment depend.

records.originHebrew: "וַאֲגַדְּלָה שְׁמֶךָ – בְּגִין דִּכְתִיב וּמִמּוֹלַדְתְּךָ", וְזֶה שֶׁאוֹמְרִים "אֱלֹהֵי יַעֲקֹב", כִּי "וַאֲגַדְּלָה שְׁמֶךָ" מְרַמֵּז עַל יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם. כִּי שֵׁם כָּל דָּבָר מוֹרֶה עַל הַחַיּוּת שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּאָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן: "וְכֹל אֲשֶׁר יִקְרָא לוֹ הָאָדָם נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה הוּא שְׁמוֹ"; וַ"אֲגַדְּלָה" לְשׁוֹן גְּדוּלָּה הוּא הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת; "וַאֲגַדְּלָה שְׁמֶךָ" – שֶׁתִּהְיֶה הַקְּדֻשָּׁה בְּהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת בְּחַיּוּת בְּלֹא הֶפְסֵק. וְהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת מִצַּד אַבְרָהָם עַצְמוֹ עֲדַיִן אֵין בְּטִיחוּת עַל הַקִּיּוּם לָעַד, כִּי הָיָה גַּם פְּסֹלֶת בְּזַרְעוֹ, וְכֵן בַּגֵּרִים שֶׁגִּיֵּיר כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל; אֲבָל יַעֲקֹב הוּא "שְׂפַת אֱמֶת תִּכּוֹן לָעַד", וְלֹא יָצָא פְּסֹלֶת מִזַּרְעוֹ, וּמֵאִתּוֹ נִתְפַּשְּׁטָה קְדֻשַּׁת יִשְׂרָאֵל לְעוֹלְמֵי עַד. וְכֵן הַגֵּרִים שֶׁבְּשֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל יְכוּנּוּ, הֵם גַּם כֵּן כְּקָטָן שֶׁנּוֹלַד, לִהְיוֹת בָּהֶם גַּם כֵּן כֹּחַ הַקִּיּוּם לָעַד. וְזֶהוּ גִּידּוּל הַשֵּׁם, דְּהַיְינוּ הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת הַחַיִּים לִזְכּוֹת לְחַיֵּי עוֹלָם, דְּכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל יֵשׁ לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא וְזוֹכִים לְחַיֵּי עוֹלָם, וְזֶה מִצַּד מִדַּת "אֱמֶת לְיַעֲקֹב", וְקַו הָאֶמְצָעִי הוּא הַמַּמְשִׁיךְ מִן הַקָּצֶה אֶל הַקָּצֶה.
records.originEnglish: “And I will make your name great—because it says, ‘and from your birthplace.’” This is what we express by saying “the God of Jacob,” for “I will make your name great” alludes to Jacob our father, of blessed memory. The name of anything indicates the vitality within it, as it is written concerning Adam: “Whatever the man would call each living creature, that was its name.” “I will make great” signifies expansion: “I will make your name great” means that holiness will expand in unceasing vitality. Expansion on Abraham’s side alone does not yet guarantee eternal endurance, for there was also an impure element among his offspring and among the converts he made, as mentioned above. But Jacob is “The lip of truth shall endure forever”: no impure element issued from his offspring, and from him the holiness of Israel spread for all eternity. Likewise, converts who are called by the name Israel are like a newly born child and also possess the power of enduring forever. This is the enlargement of the name: the expansion of life so as to attain eternal life. All Israel has a portion in the World to Come and attains eternal life. This comes from the quality of “truth to Jacob”; the middle line extends from one end to the other.
records.themeTitle: Truth means a holiness that can endure
records.themeSummary: In Jacob’s quality, spiritual expansion gains permanence. Rav Tzadok understands a great name as enduring life and the continuation of holiness through Israel’s generations.
records.targetHebrew: כִּי ג' שְׁלֹשָׁה מִינֵי חַשְׁקוּת יֵשׁ: לְתַעֲנוּגִים וַהֲנָאַת הַגּוּף; וּלְמֶמְשָׁלָה עַל הַזּוּלַת; וּלְהַשְׁאָרָה וְקִיּוּם לָעַד. וְהֵם נֶגֶד קִנְאָה, תַּאֲוָה, וְכָבוֹד: שֶׁהַכָּבוֹד – כַּאֲשֶׁר יֵשׁ לוֹ הַשְׁאָרָה לָעַד, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב מִשְׁלֵי יז, ו: "עֲטֶרֶת זְקֵנִים בְּנֵי בָנִים"; וְהֵם נֶגֶד אַבְרָהָם, יִצְחָק, וְיַעֲקֹב שֶׁבְּמִדּוֹת קְדוֹשׁוֹת: שֶׁהוּא הַחֵשֶׁק לְהִתְעַנֵּג עַל ה' חֶסֶד לְאַבְרָהָם; וְלִהְיוֹת מוֹשֵׁל בְּיִצְרוֹ גְּבוּרַת יִצְחָק; וְהַהַשְׁאָרָה לָעַד – אוּמָּה שְׁלֵימָה מְפַרְסְמִים אַחְדוּתוֹ, נֶגֶד "אֱמֶת לְיַעֲקֹב", כִּי אֱמֶת הוּא הַקִּיּוּם לָעַד, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב מִשְׁלֵי יב, יט: "שְׂפַת אֱמֶת תִּכּוֹן לָעַד", וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי רֵישׁ סַנְהֶדְרִין: דִּלְכָךְ חוֹתָמוֹ שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בּוֹ, עַיֵּין שָׁם. וְכֵן כָּל חַשְׁקוּת יַעֲקֹב וַעֲבוֹדָתוֹ – לְהוֹלִיד בָּנִים, וְנִקְרֵאת כָּל הָאוּמָּה עַל שְׁמוֹ; וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה תַּעֲנִית ה:: "יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ לֹא מֵת, מַקִּישׁ הוּא לְזַרְעוֹ". וְזֶה שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה זֹהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ פָּרָשַׁת אַחֲרֵי נז עַמּוּד א: יְשַׁעְיָה כט, כב "יַעֲקֹב אֲשֶׁר פָּדָה אֶת אַבְרָהָם", רָצָה לוֹמַר: כִּי מִצַּד מַדְרֵגוֹת אַבְרָהָם וְיִצְחָק, שֶׁהוּא רַק בַּקָּשַׁת אַהֲבַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וְיִרְאָתוֹ בְּתַכְלִית הַבֵּירוּר, לֹא הָיָה מְחַיֶּיבֶת הַהַצָּלָה מֵאוּר כַּשְׂדִּים; רַק מִצַּד מַדְרֵגַת יַעֲקֹב, שֶׁהוּא הַחֵפֶץ לְהַעֲמִיד אוּמָּה שְׁלֵימָה וְהַשְׁאָרָה לָעַד מֵהַכָּרַת כְּבוֹד ה', מִזֶּה נִמְשַׁךְ הַפִּדְיוֹן לְבַל יָמוּת וְיֹאבַד שְׁמוֹ. וְכָל אֶחָד מֵהָאָבוֹת כָּלוּל מִשְּׁלָשְׁתָּם, וּמִצַּד מַדְרֵגַת יַעֲקֹב שֶׁבּוֹ הָיָה הַפִּדְיוֹן.
records.targetEnglish: There are three kinds of desire: for pleasures and bodily enjoyment; for dominion over another; and for survival and enduring existence. These correspond to envy, desire, and honor. Honor is connected with enduring survival, as it is written, “Grandchildren are the crown of the aged” (Proverbs 17:6). In their holy qualities they correspond to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob: the desire to delight in God is “kindness to Abraham”; mastery over one’s inclination is Isaac’s might; and enduring survival—a whole nation proclaiming His unity—corresponds to “truth to Jacob.” For truth is everlasting existence, as it is written, “The lip of truth shall endure forever” (Proverbs 12:19). The Jerusalem Talmud at the beginning of Sanhedrin likewise explains that this is why it is the seal of the Holy One, blessed be He; see there. All Jacob’s desires and service were directed toward having children, and the entire nation is called by his name. Our Sages said, “Jacob our father did not die,” comparing him to his offspring (Ta’anit 5b). This is what they said concerning “Jacob, who redeemed Abraham” (Isaiah 29:22; Zohar, Acharei Mot 57a). From the levels of Abraham and Isaac, which seek the fullest refinement of love and fear of the blessed God, rescue from Ur Kasdim would not necessarily follow. But from Jacob’s level—the wish to establish a whole nation and an enduring recognition of God’s glory—redemption followed, so that Abraham would not die and his name disappear. Each patriarch includes all three qualities, and the redemption came from the quality of Jacob within Abraham.
records.explanation: Kometz HaMinchah explains what “enduring” adds to love and self-mastery. Jacob’s quality seeks the lasting continuation of the recognition of God through a people, not only the completion of an individual’s present service. This clarifies why Lech Lecha moves from a person’s name and vitality to generations, converts who enter Israel, and eternal life. The passage also specifies that all three qualities are included within each patriarch.

records.reverseThemeTitle: Seeking a recognition of God that will endure
records.reverseThemeSummary: Among the three forms of desire, Jacob’s quality seeks an enduring people who proclaim Divine unity. This lasting purpose explains why accepting a present diminution can serve a deeper completion.
records.reverseExplanation: Peri Tzadik explains what the endurance sought by Jacob’s quality means: a name expresses vitality, and the enlargement of the name is holiness extending without interruption through Israel, including those who enter as converts. This develops Kometz HaMinchah’s distinction between passing enjoyment or dominion and the lasting recognition of Divine unity.

records.originEnglish: This is what the Talmud says: “Might one conclude with all of them? The verse therefore says, ‘And you shall be a blessing’—with you they conclude.” For the meaning of “Shield of David” also comes from Abraham, to whom the Holy One, blessed be He, said, “Do not fear, Abram; I am a shield for you.” Abraham our father was afraid that he might have stumbled into some sin, as Bereishit Rabbah says: “Perhaps among those hosts I killed there was one righteous person and one who feared Heaven.” The Holy One, blessed be He, told him: Do not fear any stumbling; I am a shield for you, surrounding you on every side so that no sin can gain power over you. The holiness of King David and the Messiah also comes from you. This is why they say “Shield of David” in the Haftarah: he will be the culmination, as the holy Zohar says (III, 240b), “The conclusion is the King Messiah.” But the essential beginning comes from you. This is why they say that the blessing concludes only with you.
records.themeTitle: Why the blessing returns to Abraham at its close
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok traces the final protection associated with David and the Messiah back to Abraham. The conclusion of a blessing returns its developments to their sustaining source.

records.targetEnglish: “And you shall be a blessing—with you they conclude, and not with them.” The meaning is this. The blessing of the patriarchs is one of the long blessings, for some blessings have a long form and others a short form. A short blessing signifies the good that comes from His side; a long one signifies a person drawing out and extending that good further, as in “So may the Lord our God bring us to other appointed times and festivals.” The good that comes from His side is clear, but what a person adds of his own requires clarification. Therefore, in long blessings they instituted a further blessing of the blessed God at the conclusion, to include the good within Him. This is “with you they conclude and not with them”: complete clarification belongs to the mystery of kindness, Abraham’s level, in which there is no impurity. The world’s foundation is built on kindness, as it says, “The world shall be built through kindness” (Psalms 89:3). Although Jacob our father’s quality also contains no impurity, there have already been times when both Isaac’s and Jacob’s qualities were hidden from every living eye. Who was greater than the prophet Jeremiah and Daniel? Yet when concealment intensified, they ceased to say “mighty” and “awesome,” which are Isaac’s and Jacob’s qualities, as the Talmud teaches (Yoma 69b). But they did not cease to say “great,” Abraham’s quality, for the quality of kindness never fails.
records.explanation: Beit Yaakov explains the force of concluding specifically with Abraham by examining the structure of a long blessing. Humanly extended good needs to be returned to its Divine source, and Abraham’s kindness remains recognizable even when the other qualities are concealed. This illuminates Rav Tzadok’s claim that David’s final protection is rooted in Abraham’s beginning. The authors emphasize different aspects—unfailing kindness and protection from sin—so this is an explanatory parallel, not an identification of the two accounts.

records.reverseThemeTitle: Returning a blessing to the kindness that never ceases
records.reverseThemeSummary: A long blessing includes the good a person draws further into the world. Its conclusion returns that extension to its Divine source, and Abraham’s kindness remains even when other qualities are concealed.
records.reverseExplanation: Peri Tzadik traces the protection associated with David and the Messiah back to Abraham’s original promise. This gives a further example of a developed blessing returning at its conclusion to the beginning that sustains it. Beit Yaakov emphasizes unfailing kindness and Peri Tzadik emphasizes protection from sin; their agreement concerns the function of Abraham at the blessing’s close.

records.originEnglish: This is what is said: “Your rod and Your staff—they comfort me.” “Your staff” alludes to words of Torah, as they explained (Chagigah 14a) the verse “Support and staff, every support of bread and every support of water”: it all refers to words of Torah; see there. “Your rod” means assistance through afflictions. King David, of blessed memory, prayed that this should come through light afflictions, as it is said, “Discipline me, Lord, but with judgment”—that is, with mercy, like a father disciplining his son who raises the rod over him without striking him, with a father’s compassion.
records.themeTitle: Correction whose purpose is compassionate help
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok reads both the rod and the staff as forms of help toward Divine service. David asks that correction itself be merciful, like a father’s warning that makes an actual blow unnecessary.
records.targetHebrew: וְזֶהוּ הַשִּׂמְחָה שֶׁצָּרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת לָאָדָם בַּעֲבוֹדָתוֹ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (תְּהִלִּים ק, ב): "עִבְדוּ אֶת ה' בְּשִׂמְחָה", אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁצָּרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת גַּם כֵּן בְּיִרְאָה: "וְגִילוּ בִּרְעָדָה", מִכָּל מָקוֹם לֹא יָזוּז שִׂמְחָה זוֹ גַּם כֵּן מִנֶּגֶד עֵינָיו מַה שֶּׁהוּא זוֹכֶה לַעֲבוֹד לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְהֲיֵשׁ שִׂמְחָה גְּדוֹלָה מִזּוֹ? וְהַצַּדִּיקִים עוֹשִׂין מֵאַהֲבָה וּשְׂמֵחִין בְּיִסּוּרִין גַּם כֵּן (שַׁבָּת פח:), מֵאַחַר שֶׁמַּכִּירִין שֶׁהַכֹּל מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וְלֹא בְּמִקְרֶה חַס וְשָׁלוֹם, רַק כְּאָב הַמַּכֶּה אֶת בְּנוֹ לְהַיְישִׁירוֹ, אוֹ הָרוֹפֵא שֶׁעוֹשֶׂה דְּבָרִים מְיַיסְּרִים לַחוֹלֶה כְּדֵי לְהַחֲיוֹתוֹ, דְּוַודַּאי אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁמֵּיצַר הוּא עַכְשָׁיו – שָׂמֵחַ לְאַחַר זְמַן. וְהַמֵּבִין וּמַכִּיר גַּם בִּשְׁעַת מַעֲשֶׂה – הוּא שָׂמֵחַ.
records.targetEnglish: This is the joy a person needs in his service, as it is written, “Serve the Lord with joy” (Psalms 100:2). Although he must also have fear—“rejoice with trembling”—this joy should never leave his sight either: he has merited to serve the blessed God. Is there any greater joy than this? The righteous act from love and also rejoice in afflictions (Shabbat 88b), because they recognize that everything comes from the blessed God, not from chance, God forbid. It is like a father who strikes his son to set him on the right path, or a physician who performs painful procedures on a patient to keep him alive. Although the patient is distressed now, he will certainly be glad afterward. One who understands and recognizes this even at the time is glad then as well.
records.explanation: Resisei Layla explains the comfort in corrective help through the physician as well as the father: present pain and the purpose of preserving or restoring life are distinct. This supplies the reasoning behind Rav Tzadok’s pairing of the rod with the supportive staff. Lech Lecha adds a further emphasis to that account by recording David’s prayer that the needed correction be light and merciful.

records.reverseThemeTitle: Joy in service and the purpose of correction
records.reverseThemeSummary: Adar intensifies an enduring joy rooted in Israel’s bond with God. Within this account, corrective help can be understood through the father or physician while joy in service remains joined to awe.
records.reverseExplanation: Peri Tzadik places the same paternal image inside David’s prayer, which asks that the correction be light and merciful, even a warning without a blow. This sharpens the purpose of the father and physician images in Resisei Layla: the value lies in restoration, and the person may still ask that this good be reached with gentle means.

records.originEnglish: This is what is said: “Your rod and Your staff—they comfort me.” “Your staff” alludes to words of Torah, as they explained (Chagigah 14a) the verse “Support and staff, every support of bread and every support of water”: it all refers to words of Torah; see there. “Your rod” means assistance through afflictions. King David, of blessed memory, prayed that this should come through light afflictions, as it is said, “Discipline me, Lord, but with judgment”—that is, with mercy, like a father disciplining his son who raises the rod over him without striking him, with a father’s compassion.
records.themeTitle: Correction whose purpose is compassionate help

records.targetEnglish: “Let the young woman to whom I say, ‘Please lower your jug so that I may drink,’ and who says, ‘Drink, and I will also give your camels water’—let her be the one You have designated for Your servant Isaac.” The reason he established this sign for himself is that Isaac our father’s quality is might, and when the quality of might is clear, it is included within the quality of kindness. What appears to the eye as rage and anger in this quality resembles the teaching in Tanna de-Vei Eliyahu Rabbah, chapter 1: the blessed God acts with Israel like a father who says to his son, “I am a lion toward you; I am a bear toward you.” The father’s deeper intention in this anger is the son’s good, so that he will improve his way. Likewise, the blessed God’s intention is Israel’s good: to make awe shine in their hearts so that they follow His will. In truth, the blessed God is then filled with mercy toward Israel. But when the quality of might branches out into concealing garments, it can give rise to anger with furious cruelty, which is only evil. Thus Esau was born from Isaac; of him it is said, “Rescue my soul from the wicked man, Your sword” (Psalms 17:13). He himself does not recognize the root of the quality of might, which at its root is included within kindness. Because he does not recognize it, he has no share in it at all: he is the complete opposite of that quality’s root.
records.explanation: Beit Yaakov explains how a severe appearance can have a compassionate purpose, then explicitly distinguishes that root from cruel anger, which he calls wholly evil. This boundary is essential to the connection: Rav Tzadok’s comforting rod is directed toward restoration and mercy, and his example specifically ends without a blow. The shared image does not turn every expression of anger into holy correction.

records.originEnglish: But one must not think, God forbid, that because everything comes from the blessed God, one may follow the way of one’s heart without any effort and rely on the blessed God’s help, as in “For You are with me.” Against this, the Tanchuma concludes with the verse, “The utterance of the Lord is refined; He is a shield for all who take refuge in Him.” This means someone who exerts and strengthens himself, on his own side, to subdue his inclination with all his power, desires to take refuge beneath His wings, looks to the blessed God, and prays and pleads before the Holy One, blessed be He. He is then assured that God will not leave him in the inclination’s power. “He is a shield for all who take refuge in Him”: the evil inclination will have no power over him at all. A shield signifies that He conceals him from his enemy so that it cannot approach him at all.
records.themeTitle: Doing what one can before relying on Divine completion
records.themeSummary: The promise of protection belongs to a person who strives, seeks refuge, and prays. Rav Tzadok expressly rules out using “everything comes from God” as a reason to follow one’s desires without effort.
records.targetHebrew: (ט.) אין חוששין שמא גיררה חולדה מבית לבית וממקום למקום וכו' דא"כ אין לדבר סוף. הענין בזה, כמו שאמר כבוד אזמו"ר זללה"ה, אם האדם מצידו מנקה ומטהר ומברר עצמו עד מקום שידו מגעת. אז השי"ת מעיד עליו שהוא נמשך תמיד אחר רצונו ית', ויש לו חיבור עם אור רצונו ית'. כמו שכתוב באאע"ה (בראשית י״ז:ד׳) אני הנה בריתי אתך וגו' המול ימול וגו', אף שבאמת הדין הוא המל ימול, ואיך מל אברהם אבינו את עצמו, ומה זה שאמר לו השי"ת אני הנה בריתי אתך קודם שמל עצמו. אך הענין הוא, כיון שאאע"ה בירר עצמו עד מקום שידו מגיע, ממילא העיד עליו השי"ת שהוא מבורר וכאילו הוא נימול, כיון שלא היה בידו לברר עצמו יותר. אבל מי שאינו מברר עצמו מצידו עד מקום שידו מגיע, אלא שהוא סומך את עצמו על השי"ת שיברר אותו על הכל, אז אין השי"ת מברר אותו. וכמו שאיתא בש"ס (פסחים קיז:) בקריאת שמע גאל ישראל ודצלותא גואל ישראל, כי בק"ש מקבל עליו עול מלכות שמים, ומי שהוא מקבל עליו עול מלכות שמים מעבירין ממנו עול מלכות ועול דרך ארץ, היינו שהשי"ת יברר אותו שאין לו שום סבלנות. וזה בק"ש גאל ישראל, כי זה היה בגאולת מצרים, כמו שאנו אומרים ויוצא את עמו ישראל מתוכם לחרות עולם. ודצלותא גואל ישראל, היינו כי זה מה שהאדם בא לברר עצמו מצידו מתפלל גואל ישראל, היינו שמתפלל שיראה לו השי"ת איך שע"י עבודתו יהיה נגאל משאר גלויות. וזה אין חוששין שמא גיררה חולדה כו' דא"כ אין לדבר סוף, היינו שאין לאדם לחוש מזה מה שאין לדבר סוף, היינו שיש מקומות שאין ביכולת האדם לברר עצמו אין לו לחוש על זה, כיון שמצידו מברר עצמו עד מקום שידו מגיע. ועל אלו המקומות שאין ביכולת האדם לברר עצמו, יברר אותו השי"ת, כיון שמצידו טיהר ובירר עצמו עד מקום שביכולת האדם לברר:
records.targetEnglish: “We do not suspect that a weasel may have dragged chametz from one house to another or from one place to another … for if so, there would be no end to the matter” (Pesachim 9a). Its meaning is as my revered grandfather, of blessed memory, said: if a person, on his own side, cleanses, purifies, and clarifies himself as far as his reach extends, the blessed God then testifies that he is always drawn after His will and is connected with the light of His will. Thus it is written concerning Abraham our father, “As for Me, behold, My covenant is with you … shall surely be circumcised” (Genesis 17). In truth the law is that “one who is circumcised shall circumcise”; how, then, did Abraham circumcise himself? And why did the blessed God say, “As for Me, behold, My covenant is with you,” before he circumcised himself? The meaning is that, because Abraham had refined himself as far as his reach extended, the blessed God consequently testified that he was refined, as though he were already circumcised, since it was not in his power to refine himself further. But someone who does not refine himself, on his own side, as far as his reach extends, and instead relies on the blessed God to clarify everything for him—the blessed God does not clarify him. This corresponds to the Talmud’s teaching (Pesachim 117b): in the blessing associated with the Shema one says “Who redeemed Israel,” and in the Amidah, “Who redeems Israel.” In the Shema one accepts the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven, and one who accepts that yoke has the yoke of government and worldly occupation removed from him. That is, the blessed God will clarify that he has no burden to bear. Therefore, with the Shema one says “Who redeemed Israel,” because this occurred at the redemption from Egypt, as we say, “He brought His people Israel out from among them to everlasting freedom.” In the Amidah one says “Who redeems Israel”: as a person comes to refine himself on his own side, he prays that the blessed God show him how, through his service, he will be redeemed from the other exiles. This is “We do not suspect that a weasel may have dragged … for there would be no end to the matter.” A person need not be concerned about that which has no end: there are places in which he cannot clarify himself, and he need not fear them, provided that, on his own side, he clarifies himself as far as his reach extends. In those places beyond his capacity to clarify himself, the blessed God will clarify him, because on his own side he has purified and clarified himself as far as a person can.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef gives a practical boundary to the same principle: fully carry out the work within one’s reach, while recognizing that endlessly pursuing what lies beyond that reach cannot be the task. The chametz ruling and Abraham’s circumcision distinguish this trust from passivity. His explicit rejection of leaving all the work to God closely illuminates the closing warning in Rav Tzadok’s section.

records.themeTitle: Praying for love and awe to become one heart
records.themeSummary: The prayers ask for the heart’s own inclinations to change. Human kindness awakens kindness above, while the love and awe through which one serves are themselves received from God.

records.targetEnglish: Yet in truth, even a person’s longing for Torah and the knowledge of God is not wholly pure when his heart is not pure. The longing that naturally arises from it may be a desire like any other desire, like the desire to acquire wisdom and the like. Thus I heard concerning the verse, “The Lord was not in the wind …” (I Kings 19:11): will and ardor in love, and the tumult of awe, are all still not pure enough for the blessed God to dwell in them. Therefore the awe within the heart sets a boundary to love and constrains it so that it is only for the honor of Heaven. Their inclusion in one another is the quality of Jacob our father, who alludes to the Divine Name and to the human form in the chariot, the utmost perfection. Abraham our father himself was not completed until his tenth trial, the Binding, when he became included in Isaac’s quality, as the Zohar teaches (I, 119b), and as it is written, “Now I know that you fear God” (Genesis 22:12).
records.explanation: Tzidkat HaTzadik explains why the prayer joins love to awe instead of asking only for greater fervor. Even desire for Torah can still carry an unrefined personal motive; awe directs that love toward the honor of Heaven. Abraham’s inclusion in Isaac’s quality supplies a concrete example of the “one heart” sought in the Lech Lecha passage.

records.reverseThemeTitle: Awe prepares the heart to receive love and wisdom
records.reverseThemeSummary: Even a longing for Torah can retain an unrefined personal motive. Awe sets the boundary that directs love toward Heaven, making the heart a vessel able to receive without grasping beyond its capacity.
records.reverseExplanation: Peri Tzadik identifies a daily expression of the union sought here: the prayer “Unite our hearts to love and fear Your name.” Its account of asking God to subdue the inclination and empty evil from the heart translates Tzidkat HaTzadik’s relation between love, awe, and receptivity into the language of prayer.

records.targetEnglish: Hyssop alludes to such humility: a person recognizes that he has nothing from his own side, only what the blessed God shines upon him. As the blessed God shines upon him at each moment, so he is drawn after Him. When His will shines the quality of awe upon him, he is in awe; when He makes love shine within him, he immediately stands in love. For he recognizes well that he has nothing of his own, only what the blessed God bestows upon him. This is the meaning of the prayer, “May He place in our hearts His love and His fear”: we recognize well that even the love and awe found in our hearts are not ours, but that the blessed God places them within us. Hyssop alludes to this recognition: it is the small vav that nourishes the community of Israel, signifying humility.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim explains the inner recognition expressed by praying for love and awe: the very qualities with which a person serves are received, not independent possessions. Its account of hyssop makes the humility in Rav Tzadok’s prayer explicit. This complements the section’s account of human awakening below by clarifying the source of the heart’s capacity to respond.

records.reverseThemeTitle: Humility recognizes love and awe as gifts
records.reverseThemeSummary: Hyssop signifies the humility of one who receives each quality of service from God. Confidence grounded in this ongoing gift, rather than in possession of a fixed quality, can extend even into places of concealment.
records.reverseExplanation: Peri Tzadik explains how this recognition is expressed in the morning blessings: a person awakens kindness below, yet asks God for the love, awe, and inward subduing of the inclination with which to serve. This shows how receiving the heart’s qualities from above can coexist with an active human response, as Sod Yesharim’s image of hyssop requires.
